title: Measuring Verifier Impact in an LLM Generate→Verify→Repair Loop for Intent→Configuration NetOps Tasks
abstract: We measure how inserting a deterministic network verifier into a generate→verify→repair loop changes the verifier-detected safety-violation rate of LLM-produced device-configuration proposals. In a preregistered paired design (N=500 intent→configuration tasks) we compared (1) baseline: a single LLM proposal (gpt-5-mini) and (2) guarded: the same LLM proposal screened by a deterministic netops validator with up to one automated repair iteration. Primary outcome: verifier pass (no preregistered high/medium-severity violations). Results (complete pairs = 500): baseline passed 499/500 (0.998), guarded passed 500/500 (1.000); absolute paired success-rate difference = 0.002; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00; paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.006]. The preregistered transformation used generation_semantics = 'shared_initial_candidate' so the same initial model proposal was evaluated under both arms; the guarded arm invoked repair only when the validator flagged that shared candidate. On this synthetic, verifier-scoped corpus and this model+validator pairing the LLM produced near-ceiling proposals, so the marginal measured verifier+repair effect on the pass-rate metric is numerically small. All preregistration, execution, prompts, outputs, and validator traces are archived in the evidence bundle (representative artifact: execution/raw_results.jsonl, SHA-256 = e7c1fc4d8932389dc3e4c651cf6db08a84ba3a1cd4893b9d7d985618929ff945).

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are being applied to NetOps tasks such as intent→configuration translation, change planning, and limited automated repair. Prior system and survey work emphasizes that operational reliability depends on both model capability and surrounding engineering—validators, sandboxes, canarying, and rollback—rather than on the model alone [Beckett et al., 2017; Wei et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. Generate→verify→repair patterns are widely proposed to improve structured-output correctness, but controlled measurements that isolate the verifier contribution are limited. We preregistered and executed a paired experiment to answer a focused operational question: how much does integrating a deterministic network verifier into a generate→verify→repair loop reduce verifier-detected safety violations in LLM-generated device-configuration proposals, compared to LLM-only proposals, when tasks and topologies are canonical and restricted to verifier-modeled features? We report the preregistered design, artifact-backed execution, confirmatory analysis, and interpretation boundaries.
sections.related_work: Deterministic and formal network-verification methods (header-space analysis and route-model verifiers) can check reachability, isolation, and update-safety on configuration models [Beckett et al., 2017]. Recent NetOps/AIOps work integrates LLMs into intent-driven pipelines and emphasizes that validators and operational guardrails are essential for safe automation [Wei et al., 2025; Bilal et al., 2026]. Generate–verify–repair and verifier-assisted self-correction have been studied in code and structured-generation domains; however, published controlled ablations that quantify verifier effect size in LLM-driven NetOps pipelines are scarce. Failure-mode analyses of LLM applications (hallucination, overconfidence, tool failures) motivate guardrails [Owen, 2026]. Our contribution is a preregistered, artifact-backed paired measurement that isolates verifier+repair impact under constrained synthetic conditions.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and design: We preregistered study_id cand_7f4b9a2d_hosted_gvr_v1_2026 before execution. Confirmatory hypothesis: an LLM paired with a deterministic verifier plus one automated repair iteration will produce a lower verifier-detected safety-violation rate than the same LLM producing a single proposal without verifier feedback (paired, within-task). Sampling and tasks: 500 deterministic synthetic intent→configuration tasks were generated deterministically and stratified across canonical clusters (VLAN-change, ACL-change, static-route-change); tasks that referenced features not modeled by the validator were to be excluded (no exclusions occurred). Model and orchestration: LLM = gpt-5-mini (provider recorded as openai_responses) called via the hosted_netops_gvr_v1 adapter; deterministic validator = deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Generation semantics and shared-candidate design: preregistered generation_semantics = 'shared_initial_candidate' with independent_condition_generation = false. For each task the pipeline produced one shared LLM proposal that served as the baseline output and was also evaluated by the guarded arm; a guarded repair call was issued only when the validator flagged a preregistered high/medium-severity violation on that shared candidate. This design isolates the verifier+repair effect conditional on the same initial candidate rather than measuring verifier-guided regeneration. Execution accounting and archival paths are recorded in the execution manifest and model_configuration artifacts (execution/model_configuration.json; execution/execution_manifest.json). Analysis plan: primary estimand = paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; primary test = exact McNemar two-sided (alpha = 0.05); paired-bootstrap for 95% CI (B = 10000, seed = 1729). The analysis executor was paired_binary_analysis_v1; analysis artifacts are archived (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv and analysis/analysis_log.jsonl). Missingness, exclusions, and retries followed the preregistration.
sections.results: Execution summary and reconciliation: completed pairs = 500; model_calls_used = 501. Provider-audit stage_counts record shared_initial_generation = 500 and repair = 1 (deterministic_reconciliation provider_call_audit). Because of the shared_initial_candidate semantics, baseline outcomes were derived from the shared candidate without additional generation calls; the guarded arm reused the same candidate and triggered a repair-stage provider call only for the single task where the validator reported a preregistered high/medium-severity violation. Primary confirmatory outcomes: baseline_success_count = 499 (baseline_success_rate = 0.998); guarded_success_count = 500 (guarded_success_rate = 1.0). Paired contingency: n11 = 499, n10 = 1, n01 = 0, n00 = 0. Absolute paired success-rate difference (guarded − baseline) = 0.0020000000000000018. Exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00. Paired-bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.006] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, B = 10000). Repair activity and exclusions: zero tasks were excluded for unmodeled features; observed repair-stage provider calls = 1. Exact McNemar implementation: the analysis used the exact two-sided McNemar procedure implemented by the analysis executor as the exact binomial test on discordant pairs (treating n = n10 + n01 and testing the number of successes in one discordant cell under a Binomial(n, 0.5) two-sided rule); the analysis artifacts record test = 'exact_mcnemar_two_sided' and p_value = 1.00 (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv; analysis/analysis_log.jsonl, SHA-256 = 41f5e410f3da00fdb0258a3b5240767356a67b8d741502abe6af2396d21f88e2). Discordant-pair provenance: the run-level artifacts include per-task scoring and validator traces; the complete per-task record for the single discordant pair (validator diagnostics, repair prompt/response traces, and violating-code labels) is archived in execution/raw_results.jsonl (SHA-256 = e7c1fc4d8932389dc3e4c651cf6db08a84ba3a1cd4893b9d7d985618929ff945) and the repair-stage provider-call trace is recorded in the execution provider-call artifacts (refer to the execution manifest). The deterministic reconciliation manifest confirms provider accounting and repair-stage call count (deterministic_reconciliation.json SHA-256 = ab00aaa4ef0f3a93667b9ce281c2673e51ff5f72fc6a050d264221addfafdd00). Because the complete per-task JSON for the discordant pair is archived in the artifact bundle, reviewers and auditors can inspect the exact task identifier and the repair-trace fields at that path; the compact manuscript body reports aggregate results while pointing to the artifact entry for the specific per-task diagnostics.
sections.discussion: On this synthetic, verifier-scoped corpus and with the tested model+validator pairing the LLM produced near-ceiling correct proposals (499/500 baseline passes). Consequently measured marginal verifier+repair benefit on the pass-rate metric is numerically small (absolute improvement 0.002) and inference is limited by a ceiling effect; the exact McNemar p = 1.00 arises from only one discordant pair (n10 = 1, n01 = 0) under the exact-binomial two-sided rule. Despite the small aggregate improvement, the observed discordant case demonstrates that the guarded loop can correct rare baseline failures, confirming verifier value as a formal safety gate in at least one observed instance. Operational interpretation depends strongly on baseline error prevalence and verifier modeling coverage: in distributions where baseline error rates are higher or verifiers cover more features, verifier+repair gains on safety metrics are expected to be larger. Alternative experiment designs (e.g., verifier-feedback-guided regeneration or larger repair budgets) would answer different operational questions; those were intentionally excluded by the preregistered shared-candidate design and remain future work. The run-level artifacts permit inspection of the corrected instance, the validator-detected violation codes, and the repair-stage trace for deeper qualitative analysis.
sections.conclusion: We executed a preregistered paired experiment (N=500) comparing an LLM-only pipeline to an LLM plus deterministic verifier with one automated repair iteration under shared-initial-generation semantics. Both arms achieved near-perfect verifier pass rates (baseline 499/500, guarded 500/500), producing an absolute improvement of 0.002 (95% CI [0.0, 0.006]; exact McNemar two-sided p = 1.00). The result quantifies a ceiling-effect regime where an already-accurate LLM leaves limited measured marginal utility for a verifier on the pass-rate metric; it does not imply verifiers are unnecessary in broader, noisier, or cross-vendor production settings. Practitioners should measure proposal error prevalence and verifier coverage on realistic workloads to prioritize guardrail investments. All preregistration, execution, prompt, output, and validator artifacts are archived and available in the evidence bundle for independent verification (representative artifact: execution/raw_results.jsonl, SHA-256 = e7c1fc4d8932389dc3e4c651cf6db08a84ba3a1cd4893b9d7d985618929ff945).

limitations: Synthetic, deterministic task corpus limited to features modeled by the deterministic validator; results do not necessarily generalize to unconstrained production intents, cross-vendor CLI heterogeneity, or protocol semantics outside the verifier scope (representative task payloads show allowed_fields = {admin, mtu, vlan}).
Single model family tested (gpt-5-mini) — no claim of multi-model generality is made.
Maximum one automated repair iteration was permitted; different repair budgets or iterative regeneration strategies may change measured verifier impact.

Very high baseline pass rate (499/500) creates a ceiling effect that limits power to detect small absolute improvements on the pass-rate metric; the observed non-significant exact McNemar p = 1.00 should be interpreted in that context rather than as evidence that verifiers are universally unnecessary.
